report:
**Conclusion: probably not a firm “yes.”** Magnesium *may* reduce depressive symptoms for some adults, particularly where magnesium deficiency is present, but the evidence is preliminary and too uncertain to treat it as an established depression therapy.

A 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis pooled just seven randomized trials (325 participants) and found improvement with magnesium, but the authors note that trial findings were inconsistent and call for larger, higher-quality trials. Small samples, differing magnesium forms/doses, short follow-up, and variable study quality make the pooled result less definitive.  
https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2023.1333261/full

One often-cited 2017 trial found symptom improvement with 248 mg/day elemental magnesium (as magnesium chloride) over six weeks in adults with mild-to-moderate depression. However, it was an open-label, non-placebo-controlled crossover study—design features that can exaggerate perceived benefit.  
https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0180067

So, magnesium is reasonable to discuss with a clinician—especially if diet, medications, gastrointestinal illness, or lab testing suggest low magnesium—but should be an *adjunct*, not a replacement for proven treatments. NICE’s depression guidance recommends psychological therapies and, where appropriate, antidepressant treatment; magnesium is not a standard recommended treatment.  
https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng222/chapter/Recommendations

Safety matters: supplemental magnesium can cause diarrhea/cramping, interact with some drugs, and can be dangerous with impaired kidney function. NIH provides dosing and interaction guidance.  
https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/Magnesium-HealthProfessional/
